- Likely diagnosis is viral upper respiratory tract infection (viral bronchitis) based on typical symptom progression: sore throat followed by dry cough, mild initial fever, intermittent headache, mild wheeze and chest discomfort, and gradual symptom resolution expected (High likelihood).  
- New onset asthma or post-viral reactive airway disease is a possible consideration due to new wheeze and shortness of breath despite no prior asthma history (Moderate likelihood).  
- Atypical pneumonia (e.g., mycoplasma) cannot be ruled out completely given chest pain and ongoing cough, but absence of sputum, ongoing fever, or consolidation signs reduces likelihood (Moderate likelihood).  
- Lung cancer is very unlikely given young age and acute onset but noted due to positive maternal history; no alarming features currently present (Low likelihood).  
- Pulmonary embolism is unlikely given lack of risk factors or sudden severe symptoms (Low likelihood).  
- No contradictions between transcript and DDx; DDx supports the clinical impression from transcript.  

Management Plan  
- Provide sick note to allow additional days off work  
- Advise symptomatic management: paracetamol, adequate hydration, rest  
- Educate patient to seek urgent evaluation if symptoms worsen significantly, including increased shortness of breath, new chest pain, or other concerning signs  
- Recommend follow-up with GP if symptoms do not improve in next 4-5 days or deteriorate  
- No investigations or referrals ordered at this time  
- Consider pathology or referrals: Not recorded (no immediate indication based on assessment)

- Viral upper respiratory tract infection (viral bronchitis) – High likelihood  
  - Supported by typical symptom history, pattern, and mild clinical severity with improving trend  
- New onset asthma/reactive airway disease post-viral infection – Moderate likelihood  
  - Supported by wheeze, shortness of breath; no prior asthma history but consistent with post-viral airway hyperreactivity  
- Atypical pneumonia – Moderate likelihood  
  - Supported by chest pain and prolonged cough; no fever or sputum currently but cannot be excluded  
- Lung cancer – Low likelihood (conflict noted: positive family history but acute presentation and age argue against)  
- Pulmonary embolism – Low likelihood
